p.seg: Considering that the merit is great and the harm is little,
therefore take what is sufficient and do not change it.
Perhaps the ornate thoughts are beautifully combined,
clear and beautiful for a thousand years.
Shining like embroidered silk,
mournful like complex strings.
They must be so similar to what they imitate
that they secretly match the previous works.
Even though the idea originates from my heart,
I am apprehensive that others may precede me.
If it harms integrity and goes against righteousness,
even though I love it, I must discard it.
Sometimes the reeds send forth shoots and the points stand upright,
deviating from the crowd and possessing an exceptional quality.
Its form cannot be pursued,
its echo is difficult to tie down.
It stands alone as a solitary block,
woven from uncommon sounds.
The heart feels desolate and unmatched,
the mind hesitates and cannot be arranged.
Stone containing jade makes the mountain gleam,
water holding pearls makes the river charming.
Those hazel and prickly trees that are not trimmed
also receive glory in the gathered green.
To append "Xiàlǐ" to "Bái Xuě,"
I also aid what is considered great.
Or they entrust their words to short rhymes,
facing desolate traces and solitary inspirations.
Looking down, they are lonely and without friends,
looking up, they are vast and without support.
Like a single string stretched alone,
Although its passing and stopping are inconstant,
it is indeed difficult to navigate its uneven paths.
If one understands the changes and recognizes the order,
it is like opening a stream to receive a spring.
If one misses the opportunity and then meets it later,
one is always holding the end to continue the summit.
If one confuses the order of black and yellow (heaven and earth),
it will be murky and not fresh.
Sometimes it pressures the preceding clause,
sometimes it encroaches upon the following chapter;
sometimes the words are harmful but the reasoning is comparable,
sometimes the words are smooth but the meaning is obstructive.
Separated, they are both beautiful;
combined, they are both harmed.
Examine the highest and lowest grades in minute detail,
determine what to leave and what to remove with the utmost precision.
If it is what the scales of judgment determine,
it should certainly conform to the standard.
Sometimes the writing is elaborate and the reasoning is rich,
but the intention does not point to the appropriate place.
Extremely lacking duality,
and nothing more can be added.
Establishing a single phrase to occupy the essence,
is the key point of the entire piece.
Although the many words are organized,
they must rely on this to achieve results.
Dignified bearing and detailed posture,
every movement forming a spectacle,
this comes from the beauty of one's physique.
Thinking, knowledge, □ love's forward progress,
power always present,
it is fitting to □ praise them.
During the time of Xia □ Rong and bandit turmoil,
news and inquiries were not fully known.
○ A reproduction of the "Píngfù Tiě" of Lù Jī by the Cultural Relics Publishing House in September 1961.
Untitled
"Untitled"
Emperor Wén's power was greater than that of the Three Kingdoms,
but he himself ended up facing north,
though it is said he had no time,
the kingdom's foundation was already secure.
○ From "Chū Xué Jì", Volume 9.
Discussion on Limiting Judgments in the History of Jin
"Discussion on Limiting Judgments in the History of Jin"
The three ancestors were actually always ministers,
therefore, the record of their affairs as ministers,
cannot but be treated as biographies,
this is what is meant by recording the truth.
But their names are the same as emperors,
therefore, from the registers of emperors,
it is impossible not to call them "Annals",
this is the meaning of posthumously bestowing kingship.
○ From "Chū Xué Jì", Volume 21.
containing a clear song but finding no response.
Or they entrust their words to weary tones,
saying things that are merely wasteful and not refined.
Mixing the beautiful and the ugly to form a body,
burdening good qualities to become flaws.
Like a lower pipe being flawed,
therefore, although it responds, it is not harmonious.
Or they abandon reason to preserve uniqueness,
merely seeking emptiness and pursuing the subtle.
Their words lack emotion and love,
their diction floats and does not return [to the subject].
Like a string that is thin and the frets are close,
therefore, although it is harmonious, it is not sad.
Or they are unrestrained to achieve harmony,
striving for cacophony and gaudiness.
Merely pleasing the eye and occasionally vulgar,
thus the sound is high but the melody is low.
Awakening to "Fáng Lù" and "Sāng Jiān" (titles of lewd songs),
and although sad, they are not elegant.
Or they are pure and empty to achieve subtlety,
always removing煩 (fán, vexation) and eliminating extravagance.
They lack the lingering taste of dàgēng (大羹, plain broth),
Matching the pure and overflowing sounds of Zhū Xuán's zither.
Though sung but once, sighed over thrice,
inherently elegant and not gaudy.
As for the art of fullness and leanness,
the forms of bowing and raising,
adapting to suit the occasion,
each melody holding subtle emotions.
Sometimes seemingly clumsy, yet hinting at skill,
sometimes simple in principle, yet light in expression.
Sometimes borrowing from the old, yet becoming new,
sometimes following the murky, yet becoming clearer.
Sometimes, upon a glance, one must scrutinize,
sometimes, only after careful study, does one become refined.
It is like a dancer following the rhythm, throwing up their sleeves,
a singer responding to the strings, sending forth their voice.
This is something that Lún Biǎn could not put into words,
and therefore is not something that flowery rhetoric can master.
Broadly speaking of verbal embellishments and literary principles,
these are truly what I, Your Servant, admire.
Refining the common faults of worldly affairs,
recognizing the virtues of previous scholars.
Although deeply rooted in a skillful mind,
they may sometimes be bestowed clumsily, upon ignorant eyes.
Those beautiful and precious writings,
are as common as beans in the Central Plains.
Like a bellows that never runs dry,
To be nurtured together with Heaven and Earth.
Though luxuriant in this world,
alas, they do not fill my hands.
I worry about the repeated emptiness of the water jar,
and I am troubled by the difficulty in composing grand pronouncements.
Therefore, I stumble along the low wall,
uttering vulgar sounds to satisfy the tune.
I always leave regret to end the poem,
how could I embrace fullness and be content?
I fear being covered in dust like a clay pot,
and I consider being ridiculed for sounding jade.
As for the meetings of feeling and response,
the principles of flow and obstruction,
their coming cannot be stopped,
their going cannot be halted.
They are hidden as if shadows extinguished,
they are acted upon like echoes rising.
Considering the sharp efficiency of the heavenly mechanism,
why would they be confused and not organized?
Thoughts like wind arise from the breast,
words like springs flow from the lips and teeth.
Luxuriant and abundant,
only brush and silk can imitate them.
Literary patterns shine brightly overflowing the eyes,
sounds tinkle clearly filling the ears.
When the six emotions are stagnant at the bottom,
the will goes forth but the spirit remains,
Still as a withered tree,
Open as a dried-up stream.
Grasping the ethereal soul to explore the profound,
Focusing the vital spirit in self-seeking.
The principle grows obscure and ever concealed,
Thoughts twist and turn as if being drawn out.
Therefore, some exhaust their emotions and have much regret,
Others follow their inclinations and have little blame.
Though this thing is within me,
It is not something my strength can force.
So I often stroke my empty breast and lament,
I do not yet understand the reason for its opening and closing.
This writing's function,
Is surely what all principles depend on.
Spreading ten thousand *lǐ* without obstruction,
Connecting hundreds of millions of years as a ferry.
Below, it leaves a model for future generations,
Above, it observes the images in the ancients.
Rescuing Wén and Wǔ from imminent fall,
Proclaiming fame so it is not extinguished.
No road is so far that it does not extend,
No principle is so subtle that it is not organized.
Matching the moistening of clouds and rain,
Resembling the transformations of ghosts and spirits.
Enduring on metal and stone, its virtue broadens,
Flowing through pipes and strings, it renews daily.
《Gǎn Shí Fù》
Alas, the nature of winter's atmosphere,
how chilling and desolate it is!
The sky is distant and exceedingly high,
the fog dense and enveloping in all directions.
The night is long and seemingly endless,
the day is short and easily fades.
Spreading layers of luxuriant clouds,
falling, scattering snowflakes.
The ice is bitterly cold, whether sleeping or waking,
the wind is unrestrained and wildly blows.
The bare branches whistle,
the falling leaves flutter desolately.
The mountains are cavernous, holding sorrow,
the rivers winding, embracing dryness.
Gazing at the eight cardinal directions, all is vast and blurred,
the entire universe is desolate and empty.
Now that the season is so bleak,
how can the myriad things find joy?
The fish faintly seek mates,
the beasts stand tall, gathering together.
The ape lets out a long howl in the treetops,
the bird cries loudly at the edge of the clouds.
How much more does my heart hold sorrow,
constantly seeing things and adding to my bitterness.
Experiencing the alternating feelings of the four seasons,
I grieve that the year is already cold.
Clutching my wounded heart, I sob,
Wàng yǒng lù ér wánlán.
Thick frost forms in the dew-covered room,
condensing traveling rain at the root of clouds.
○《Selections from the Northern Hall》152.
"Rhapsody on a Hero, with Preface"
Now, the foundation for establishing virtue is constant,
but the paths for achieving merit are not the same.
Why is this?
Those who measure things by their own hearts exist within themselves,
while those who accomplish tasks based on external things are bound by them.
Those who exist within themselves,
their rise and fall are limited to their own domain;
those who are bound by external things,
their abundance or scarcity depends on what they encounter.
A falling leaf awaits a gentle breeze to fall,
and the power of the wind is quite weak;
Mèngcháng (Lord Mèngcháng) encountered Yōngmén and wept,
but the emotion evoked by the zither was trivial.
Why?
Because the leaf that is about to fall does not require a strong wind,
and the tears that are about to fall are insufficient to amplify mournful sounds.
Therefore, if the time is ordained by Heaven,
and the principles are exhausted by the people,
an ordinary man can achieve the merits of sages and worthies,
and a man of small capacity can establish the deeds of martyrs.
Thus it is said, "Talent is not half that of the ancients,
yet accomplishments have already doubled,"
This was truly obtained from the circumstances of the time.
Throughout history,
there have been those who, relying on temporary achievements, have occupied positions like those of Yī Yǐn 伊尹 and Zhōu Gōng 周公.
The concept of "self" clinging to oneself
is a burden even for the wise;
the concept of "things" belonging to other things
is a sentiment that even insects possess.
To take the measure of one's self and possess extraordinary achievements,
where the imperial regalia reflect in their gaze,
and all things follow their inclinations,
their hearts delight in the ease of normalcy,
and their ears are filled with flattering words,
how could they recognize that merit lies outside oneself,
and responsibility exceeds one's abilities?
Furthermore, to love honor and hate disgrace
is the great aspiration of all living beings;
to be wary of fullness and harm from superiors,
is something from which even ghosts and spirits cannot escape.
When the ruler holds the constant power,
the world submits to his great integrity,
hence it is said, "Can Heaven be hated?"
Yet there are those who wear ornate clothes and carry halberds,
standing beneath the temple gates,
seizing the banner to rally the masses,
and agitating in the fields and paths.
How much more so those who make decrees on behalf of the ruler,
and from below, judge all things!
Bestowing widespread favors is not enough to overcome resentment,
diligently creating benefits is not enough to compensate for harm.
Therefore, it is said, "He who chops in place of a master craftsman
will surely injure his own hand."
Moreover, if authority originates from the Níng family,
loyal ministers will be filled with righteous indignation;
if sacrifices are solely the affair of the "one man"
(the ruler), the ruler will not long endure such a situation.
Thus, Jūn Shì was discontented,
displeased with Gōng Dàn's actions;
Gāo Píng glared,
regarding Bó Lù's power with suspicion.
And King Chéng did not dismiss suspicion and resentment from his mind,
Emperor Xuān felt as if he carried thorns on his back.
Were these things not so?
Alas!
His virtue shone upon the four directions,
no virtue was richer;
the king called him "Uncle Father," no one was more intimate;
he ascended to the Emperor's heavenly position,
no merit was greater;
he maintained his integrity until death,
no loyalty was greater.
Yet he was subjected to dangerous circumstances and
barely preserved himself.
Thus, for Yī Shēng to embrace clear promises and meet with execution,
for Wén Zǐ to harbor loyalty and respect and meet the sword,
Gù qí suǒ yě.
Speaking from this perspective,
even with such excellent qualities of profound sagacity and affectionate reverence,
and such great virtue and utmost loyalty,
they still cannot gain the trust of the ruler's heart,
nor silence the criticism of the multitude.
Beyond this point,
how can one expect success!
The principles of safety and danger
can certainly be understood.
Furthermore, how much more so for those who greedily pursue great fame while violating the prohibitions of Daoism,
and employ their limited talents to attempt what even sages and wise men found difficult!
Personal danger arises from excessive power,
yet they do not know to relinquish power to seek safety;
calamity accumulates from excessive favor,
yet they do not know to decline favor to invite blessings.
Seeing that the people are plotting against them,
they reinforce palace guards
to increase an unsought authority;
fearing that the populace will not submit,
they implement harsh laws and severe punishments
to buy the resentment of broken hearts.
Consequently, their authority dwindles to threatening the ruler,
and resentment spreads throughout all levels of society.
The hearts of the people are declining day by day,
a crisis is about to erupt,
yet they are still reclining and staring about,
thinking they are sufficient to boast to the world,
Laughing at the ancients for their lack of skill,
Forgetting one's own clumsy deeds,
Knowing that past achievements are worthy of pride,
Unaware that success and failure are a matter of timing.
Therefore, when matters reach their limit and fortune is exhausted,
One is certain to fall;
When the wind rises and dust gathers,
The calamity that arrives is often severe.
The sage avoids letting merit and fame exceed himself,
And detests allowing favor and emolument to surpass their proper measure,
Precisely because of this.
Now, the greatest of desires,
Is something shared by both the wise and the foolish,
And the wandering son pursues a high position while still alive,
The ambitious man thinks of leaving a name behind him after death,
The portion received at birth,
Is just this and nothing more.
Now, of worldly achievements,
None is greater than fame;
Of power that shakes the ruler,
None is stronger than position;
To do as one pleases without opposition,
No desire is more compliant.
Assuming this person had some understanding of the Way of Heaven,
Knew that perfection cannot be increased,
And fullness is difficult to maintain for long,
He would transcendently withdraw himself,
Having made a respectful bow and withdrawn,
then his towering virtue would be revered like that of previous sages,
and his vast influence would surpass all who came after,
while his great desires would be fully satisfied,
and his ultimate joy would remain as it was before.
His integrity would become more effective, and his virtue would become more expansive;
his life would become more leisurely, and his reputation would become more illustrious.
If this is not done,
then the other will surely be obscured.
Then the traces of rivers and seas will be filled in, becoming mere trickles,
and the flaw of a single basketful will accumulate into mountains.
His name will be listed among the wicked and stubborn,
and his body will suffer the pain of bitter poison.
Would this not be a mistake?
Therefore, I write this poem,
hoping that some in future generations will awaken.
In the world, there are heroic men
who encounter a state in decline.
They seize the return of the age's exhaustion,
and meet at the assembly of all understanding.
If the time arrives and the principle is exhausted,
it is like snapping dry twigs and shaking off decay.
They take advantage of Heaven and Earth's movement,
so that ordinary talents achieve great deeds.
Therefore, their ceremony reaches the highest standards,
and their garments are exceedingly brilliant and revered.
They arrange the universe like the North Star,
Living in a fragrant orchid room, resembling the Guì Gōng (桂宮, Cassia Palace on the moon).
Holding the Yù Héng (玉衡, jade sighting tube of an astronomical instrument) and the Shū Jí (樞極, the pivot of the heavens),
Governing all things within the palm of my hand.
Even the robust and vigorous way of Heaven,
Must inevitably preserve itself when the time comes.
The sun does not fail to decline after midday,
And the moon—how can it not wane after being full?
Following the perilous track of an overturned cart,
I laugh at those who went before and did not complete the task.
If I had known the danger and retreated,
Hastened back to my domain and restrained myself,
I would have turned the celestial sphere to bid a long farewell,
Surveyed all things and made a lofty bow.
Ceasing my ambitions with drifting clouds,
How could blame and ill fortune accumulate?
But I pushed a mountain to cause my own downfall,
Lamenting the disaster—how far it has reached!
"Ode to the Melon"
Excellent indeed is the virtue of the melon,
Surpassing all other fruits in excellence.
It embodies the pure blessings of harmony and moderation,
Spreading its abundant growth in rich fields.
Planted at the beginning of the fragrant spring,
It welcomes the red summer and prolongs its life.
Displaying its long and unceasing tendrils,
Extending the beautiful, unbroken line of small melons.
Reaching towards Guǎng Wǔ (廣武) with long vines,
Càn yān jiē yǐ yún lián. (Bright smoke connects and merges with the clouds.)
Gǎn jiā shí ér cù jié, (Grateful for the auspicious time, urging forth the nodes,)
Méng huì zhān ér zēng xiān. (Receiving gracious dew and increasing freshness.)
Ruò nǎi fēn fū zá cuò, (As for their abundant blossoming and intricate intermingling,)
Yù yuè pó suō, (Luxuriant and pleasing, swaying gracefully,)
Fā bǐ shì cǐ, (Sprouting there and flourishing here,)
Dié xiāng jīng guò, (Alternately passing each other,)
Xī lǎng rì yǐ yì yào, (Sparkling and shining in the bright sun,)
Shàn hé fēng qí rú bō, (Fanning a gentle breeze like waves,)
Yǒu gě léi zhī diàn jí, (There are the lattices of kudzu vines reaching,)
Xiāng jiāo liáo zhī zhòng duō, (And the numerousness of fragrant Sichuan pepper,)
Fā jīn róng yú xiù qiào, (Displaying golden splendor in elegant beauty,)
Jié yù shí yú róu kē, (Forming jade-like fruit on supple branches,)
Bì cuì jǐng yǐ zì yù, (Concealing verdant scenes for their own nurturing,)
Zhuì xiū jīng ér xīng luó. (Adorning slender stems, scattered like stars.)
Fú qí zhǒng zú lèi shù, (As for their kinds and varieties,)

Zé yǒu kuò lóu, dìng táo, huáng qiú, bái zhuàn, jīn wén, mì tǒng, xiǎo qīng, dà bān, xuán gàn, sù wǎn, lí shǒu, hǔ fán, (There are Trichosanthes, the Dìng peach, yellow melon, white melon, golden pattern, honey tube, small green, large spotted, black shank, plain bowl, leopard head, tiger paw,)
Dōng líng chū yú Qín gǔ, (Dōnglíng melon comes from the valleys of Qín,)
Guì suǐ qǐ yú Wū shān. (Guìsuǐ melon originates from Wū Mountain.)
Wǔ sè bǐ xiàng, (Five colors compare in appearance,)
Shū xíng yì duān, (Diverse shapes and different forms,)
Huò jì mào yǐ biǎo nèi, (Some use fine appearance to reveal inner quality,)
Huò huì xīn ér chǒu yán, (Some have kind hearts but ugly faces,)
Huò shū wén ér bào lǜ, (Some spread patterns and embrace green,)
Huò pī sù ér huái dān. (Some wear white and harbor red.)
Qì hóng xì ér jù fēn, (Their aroma, whether rich or subtle, is always fragrant,)
Tǐ xiū duǎn ér bì yuán. (Their form, whether long or short, is always round.)
Fāng yù liè qí chōng táng, (Fragrance, rich and intense, fills the hall,)
Wèi qióng lǐ ér bù yàn. (Flavor, fully explored, is never cloying.)
Dé hóng jì yú jī kě, (Their virtue greatly helps with hunger and thirst,)
Dào yīn liú ér guì jiàn. (Their way flows generously, for both noble and humble.)
Ruò fú zhuó yǐ hán shuǐ, (If washed with cold water,)
Cuì yǐ xià líng, (Quenched with summer ice,)
Scroll 1
*Wén Fù Bìng Xù* (Rhapsody on Literature with Preface)
Whenever I observe the works of talented scholars,
I can somewhat grasp their intentions.
Indeed, their unrestrained speech and choice of words
undergo many transformations.
Their beauty and ugliness, their likes and dislikes,
can be discussed.
Each time I compose,
I especially see my own feelings.
I am constantly troubled by the fact that my thoughts do not match the object,
and my writing does not capture my thoughts.
For it is not the understanding that is difficult,
but the execution.
Therefore, I compose the "Wén Fù" to describe the magnificent writing of former scholars.
I also discuss the advantages and disadvantages of composing, and the reasons for them.
In the future, it may be said that I have thoroughly exhausted its subtleties.
As for wielding an axe to hew an axe handle,
although the principle is not far to seek,
as for the variations that come from practice,
it is truly difficult to capture them in words.
What I am able to express,
is all contained herein.
I pause in the central region to contemplate profoundly,
and nourish my emotions and will with classical texts.
I follow the four seasons and sigh at the passage of time,
and gaze upon the myriad things and my thoughts become confused.
I grieve at the falling leaves in the strong autumn,
and rejoice at the soft branches in the fragrant spring.
My heart trembles with the thought of frost,
and my spirit soars as it looks upon the clouds.
I sing of the brilliant deeds of virtuous generations,
and recite the pure fragrance of my ancestors.
I wander in the forest of literature,
and admire the beauty of its flourishing embellishments.
Moved, I put down the scroll and pick up the brush,
to express myself in this writing.
In the beginning,
all gather their sight and listen attentively,
indulging in thought and seeking information from all sides,
Galloping wildly to the eight limits of the universe,
the mind wanders ten thousand *rèn* high.
Its accomplishment lies in
emotions, which become increasingly vivid in a hazy state;
objects, which become clearer and advance reciprocally;
draining the essence of myriad words,
rinsing with the fragrant and moist essence of the Six Arts,
floating in the heavenly abyss, finding peace in the current,
cleansing in the lower spring, soaking in the depths.
Thereupon, profound words burst forth in joy,
like a swimming fish taking the bait and emerging from the deep of the abyss;
floating phrases come in flocks,
like a soaring bird, entangled by a tether, falling from the steepness of layered clouds.
Gathering the fragmentary texts of a hundred generations,
collecting the lost melodies of a thousand years,
bidding farewell to the morning blossoms that have already unfolded,
initiating the evening beauty that has not yet bloomed,
observing the past and present in an instant,
embracing the four seas in a breath.
Then, selecting meanings and arranging them in order,
examining phrases and placing them in ranks,
those who cherish the vision all knock (on the door),
those who harbor the echo all pluck (the strings).
Some shake the leaves by means of the branches,
some seek the source by following the waves.
Some start from the hidden to reach the obvious,
some seek the easy and find the difficult.
Perhaps like a tiger's transformation, the beasts are disturbed;
perhaps like a dragon appearing, the birds are in disarray.
Sometimes it is proper and easy to implement;
sometimes it is rugged and uneasy.
Exhausting a clear mind to concentrate thoughts,
diminishing numerous concerns to formulate words,
encompassing heaven and earth within its form,
subduing all things at the tip of the brush.
Initially hesitant at the dry tip,
ultimately flowing freely from the moistened brush.
Reason supports substance to establish the trunk,
elegance hangs branches to form abundance.
Believing that emotions and appearances are not different,
therefore every change is apparent in the expression.
When thoughts involve joy, one must smile;
when expressing grief, one can only sigh.
Sometimes holding the writing tablet with ease,
sometimes holding the brush with a distant gaze.
Oh, this affair is so enjoyable,
indeed esteemed by sages and worthies.
Demanding existence from nothingness,
knocking on silence to seek sound,
enclosing vastness within a foot of silk,
expressing abundance from an inch of heart.
Words expanding to become vast,
thoughts pressing to become deeper,
scattering the fragrant *ruí* flowers with rich aroma,
The green branches flourish in the dense forest,
Càn, the wind flies swiftly and fiercely,
Dense clouds rise in the Hànlín (Imperial Academy).
Bodies have myriad differences,
Things are immeasurable,
Confused and rapid,
Their forms are difficult to describe.
Words follow talent to display skill,
Intentions manage contracts to become artisans,
Striving between existence and non-existence,
Not yielding on what is shallow and deep.
Although departing from the square to escape to the round,
Hoping to exhaust shapes and completely capture appearances.
Therefore, those who boast of seeing appreciate extravagance,
Those who satisfy the heart value appropriateness,
Those whose words are exhaustive have no narrowness,
Those whose discussions are thorough are only broad.
Poetry is ornate and beautiful because of emotion,
Rhapsodies are bright and clear because of their focus on describing objects.
Inscriptions adorn texts to match the substance,
Laments are lingering and sorrowful.
Inscriptions are broad and concise yet gentle and refined,
Admonitions are full of pauses and clear and strong.
Eulogies are leisurely and refined,
Treatises are precise and clear and fluent.
Memorials are straightforward, clear, and elegant,
Persuasions are brilliant and deceitful.
Although distinctions lie herein,
it also prohibits the wicked and controls the unrestrained.
The main thing is that the words express the meaning and the reasoning is sound,
therefore, there is no need for redundancy.
Its forms are varied and colorful,
its structure changes frequently.
Its understanding of meaning emphasizes ingenuity,
and its employment of language values beauty.
And with the alternation of sounds,
it's like the intermingling of five colors.
